options: An atom that has gained or lost electrons, so it carries a charge
An atom with a different number of neutrons
A molecule with an extra atom
A neutral atom exactly like any other
questions.explanation: An ion is an atom that has gained or lost electrons, so it carries an electric charge.
questions.misconception: A different neutron count is an ISOTOPE, not an ion — the ion is specifically about electrons changing, which creates a charge.

questions.prompt: Sodium loses one electron and becomes Na⁺. Why is Na⁺ positive?
options: It now has more protons than electrons
It now has more electrons than protons
questions.explanation: Losing an electron leaves more protons than electrons, so the atom carries a net positive charge.
questions.misconception: Protons are never lost in ion formation, and more electrons would make it negative — losing electrons is exactly what makes a cation positive.

questions.prompt: Chlorine gains one electron and becomes Cl⁻. Why is Cl⁻ negative?
options: It now has more electrons than protons
It now has more protons than electrons
questions.explanation: Gaining an electron leaves more electrons than protons, so the atom carries a net negative charge.
questions.misconception: Gaining protons is impossible in normal chemistry — the charge comes purely from the extra electron, which makes the atom negative.

questions.prompt: What happens when a positive ion and a negative ion meet?
options: They attract and bond — building compounds like salt
They combine into a new element
questions.explanation: Opposite charges attract — Na⁺ and Cl⁻ lock together in an ionic bond, building table salt.
questions.misconception: Opposite charges attract (they never repel), and the ions do not revert or fuse into new elements — they hold together as a charged compound.
